newsitem.title: Bosnia: First U.S. troops enter Bosnia to cover pullout.
newsitem.headline: First U.S. troops enter Bosnia to cover pullout.

text.p: The first units of a 5,000-strong U.S. army force assigned to cover a withdrawal of American peacekeeping troops from Bosnia entered the country on Tuesday, witnesses said.

Almost two dozen U.S. army trucks and Humvee all-terrain vehicles along with two buses rolled across a U.S. military pontoon bridge spanning the Sava River between Zupanja, Croatia and Orasje, Bosnia, at midday.
Some 15,000 troops of the U.S. 1st Armoured Division poured into Bosnia at the same crossing 10 months ago for a year-long mission to help NATO enforce the 1995 Dayton peace treaty.
A total of 500 advance troops in the covering force, also part of the 1st Armoured, were expected to enter Bosnia by Tuesday night with the rest flowing in over the next six weeks.
They will secure a pullout of the main American peacekeeping force, due to be completed early in 1997.
A U.S. Army statement said the vanguard of the covering force arriving on Tuesday included infantry, field artillery, air defence, engineering and support units.
The first few units of the peacekeeping contingent, part of a 53,000-strong NATO-led force (IFOR), began to leave Bosnia last week bound for their European headquarters in Germany.

"My soldiers are very optimistic and they've been trained for this (coverage) mission throughout the summer. We have done a lot of coordination with the 1st Armoured Division," Colonel Michael Thompson, 45, told reporters.
"We are starting the transition processes as we reshape the forces for the 1st Armoured Division," said Thompson, commander of the 2nd Brigade Combat Team and a native of Wyoming.

NATO's one-year peace enforcement mission, which separated Bosnia's ethnic armies without bloodshed, expires on December 20 under terms of the 1995 Dayton peace treaty reached by Serb, Croat and Moslem leaders with U.S. mediation.

But NATO officials say some kind of "follow-on" force, including U.S. troops, will be needed next year because the peace implementation process, notably in the civilian political sector, remains fragile.
U.S. President Bill Clinton promised the American people ahead of elections on November 5 that U.S. troops in the IFOR mission would get out of Bosnia on schedule.
The start of the withdrawal had been set back by a delay in post-war municipal elections, now set for late November, which NATO troops must secure against possible nationalist violence.
Tens of thousands of IFOR troops ensured that Bosnia's first post-war general elections held last month were orderly.
The "covering force" of 5,000 U.S. troops is due to stay in Bosnia until next March at the latest.
